did_you_know.text: The vision opens with the Lord standing beside the altar and commanding that the capitals be struck so that the thresholds will shake. This depicts judgment beginning at the Temple and affecting the people.
The chapter emphasizes that there is no hiding place from the Lord’s decree: even if they dig down to Sheol or climb up to heaven, the Lord’s hand will reach them.
Carmel and the sea are not places of refuge either: those hiding in Carmel will be searched out, and those in the depths of the sea will be struck by the serpent the Lord commands.
The Lord is described as touching the earth so that it melts and trembles; the whole land rises and sinks like the Nile in Egypt.

The verse presents the Lord as building His upper chambers in the heavens and establishing His vault over the earth, and as calling for the waters of the sea and pouring them over the face of the land.
The Lord reminds them that other nations have also been moved from their lands: Israel was brought up from Egypt, the Philistines from Caphtor, and Aram from Kir.

Alongside the announcement that the sinful kingdom will be destroyed, the text says that the house of Jacob will not be completely destroyed. The chapter thus distinguishes between judgment and the remnant that will be preserved.

Israel is compared to grain shaken in a sieve: the Lord will shake the house of Israel among the nations, yet not a single pebble will fall to the ground. The process is therefore portrayed as sifting and separating.
After the words of judgment comes a promise to restore David’s fallen shelter: its breaches will be repaired, its ruins rebuilt, and it will be reconstructed.
The vision of redemption is described through extraordinary agricultural abundance: plowing and harvesting will follow one another closely, and the mountains will drip with sweet wine.
